steps: Check fireplace size & hearth

Opening at least 29-1/2" wide at front, 24" at rear, 16" deep and 21-1/4" high, with adequate load bearing capacity. Non-combustible masonry hearth under the full unit and vent pipe, extending 16" beyond the opening.
Permit & approved fireplace

Get a permit and the inspection requirements; a WETT (Canada) or HEARTH (USA) certified installer is strongly recommended. Masonry fireplace per NFPA 211 (installation to CAN/CSA-B365), or a factory-built zero-clearance fireplace and chimney listed to UL 127 or ULC S610.
Prepare the masonry fireplace

Repair cracks or loose mortar, clean the chimney, and lock the damper open or remove it. Don't remove bricks or mortar; masonry or steel (damper plate included) may come out of the smoke shelf and adjacent damper frame only if needed for the liner, and only if that won't weaken the structure of the fireplace and chimney or reduce protection for combustible materials below what the National Building Code requires. Fasten the supplied metal tag to the back wall if the fireplace was modified.
Full flue liner (required in Canada)

Feed a 3" or 4" stainless liner from the chimney top through the damper area, attach it to the Ash Cleanout box adapter with screws and level with the rear adjusting legs. Flash the top, then fit a rain cap and storm collar.

1. Measure the chimney height from the top of the existing flue to the floor of the hearth; this leaves extra liner for flashing and the rain cap.
  2. Feed the stainless steel liner from the top of the chimney, through the damper area and into the fireplace cavity.
  3. Push the insert in, attach the flex liner to the stove's Ash Cleanout box adapter and secure with screws. Push it close to its final position and level it with the rear adjusting legs.
  4. Measure, trim and shape a top flashing to fit the existing flue, with a 1" to 1-1/2" overlap on each side. Seat it firmly against the tile, screw the flashing collar to the liner and caulk the gap with RTV silicone.
  5. Attach a rain cap to the end of the liner; a storm collar should be used.

The liner runs all the way from the insert flue to the top of the chimney, with a sealing plate at the top. The liner standard printed on this page differs from p. 19; see the Venting card.
Direct flue connection (USA only)
Run the liner from the insert into the first chimney flue tile, allowing 12 inches extra length, and seal around the pipe. A clean-out door may be required under local codes.

1. Measure from the first chimney flue liner to the top of the insert. Allow 12 inches extra length of liner to go into the flue tile.
  2. Feed the stainless steel liner through the damper area and into the first chimney flue tile. Seal around the pipe to the chimney.
  3. Push the insert in, attach the flex liner to the stove's Ash Cleanout box adapter and secure with screws. Push it close to its final position and level it with the rear adjusting legs.

Figure 13 on this page shows the sealed-flue layout as a drawing.
Factory-built fireplace

Full stainless rigid or flexible liner (UL1777 U.S. / ULC S635 Canada) secured to the flue collar and the chimney top; seal the surround to the fireplace front or seal the damper area. Don't block louvers or cooling-air ports; only external trim and the chimney damper may come out.
Outside air (recommended)

Optional, but recommended; required where local building codes call for it. 2"(51mm) ID non-combustible pipe to the air intake: through the ash clean-out with a vented grill, a hole through the back of the fireplace, or a 2" flex liner up the chimney. Exterior intake substantially below the flue termination, with a screen cover.
Thermostat (optional)

Unplug; remove the surround, the right cabinet side and the 2 screws holding the main board; land the two low-voltage thermostat wires on the double screw terminal block at the top of the board. Keep the thermostat clear of radiant heat, drafts and duct air.
Set the damper on first firing

Vacuum gauge on the port by the ash pan door, both trims at 3. After 15-20 min. on high, set the damper for 0.10-0.12 n.w.c.; on Heat Level 1 after 5-10 minutes expect 0.09" to 0.11", or adjust the combustion blower trim.

1. Fit a low pressure digital vacuum gauge or magnehelic, with a sealed 1/8" metal probe, into the port above or to the side of the ash pan door.
  2. Find the damper against the back of the Air Jacket and loosen its locking screw.
  3. Start the unit. Check that the combustion blower and auger trims are both set to 3 (middle position).
  4. After 15-20 min. on high, adjust the damper to read 0.10-0.12 n.w.c. Pull it out toward the outside of the stove to increase firebox vacuum; push it in to reduce it.
  5. Turn down to Heat Level 1 (LOW), wait 5-10 minutes and read again: 0.09" to 0.11". If not, adjust the combustion blower trim: hold the hidden button under position 7 and use the heat level up/down buttons (factory setting 3; the light that is out shows the setting).
  6. Tighten the damper locking screw and install the surround.

Pellet quality varies, so the damper may need adjusting from time to time: closed slightly if the stove keeps going out on low, opened slightly if the liner keeps building up ash and clinkers. This should be done by a qualified installer or service technician.
Surround & control panel

Bolt surround parts A, B and C together, lower the surround around the stove, connect the ribbon cable and hook the panels into the bracket slots. Mount the control panel with the Keps nuts and push the unit back until the surround meets the fireplace.

1. Lay surround parts A, B and C face down on a flat, non-marring surface and fasten them with the 1/4" x 1/2" bolts and nuts through the holes at points D.
  2. Stand the assembly upright and check that the front face is flat and even at the joints.
  3. Move it around the stove, lowering it carefully to avoid scratching the paint. Attach the ribbon cable to the main circuit board.
  4. Engage the panel hooks in the slots on the surround brackets and push down to lock.
  5. Unwrap the control panel (packed in plastic in the back of the unit), remove the Keps nuts from the studs on the back of the surround, fit the panel over the studs and secure it with the Keps nuts.
  6. Push the entire appliance back until the surround contacts the fireplace structure.

The supplied leveling legs thread in from underneath to stabilize the front or back on uneven or dropped surfaces.

light.title: Starting and stopping the stove
light.html:
Before each start, check that the holes in the burn-pot liner are clear and that the liner sits pressed back against the igniter tube.

Starting

  1. First start, or the stove ran out of pellets? Prime the liner: put a handful of pellets in its middle, or hold down the Auger button to run the auger.
  2. Press ON/OFF. The Power light turns red and a 15 minute lighting sequence begins: the auger loads the burn pot, the igniter lights the pellets, then feeding resumes.
  3. Once it's lit, the Power light turns green. The stove burns at the level shown on the heat level display.

Some smoke inside the firebox during light-up is expected.

Don't restart mid-cycle. The burn pot will overload with pellets. If it isn't lit after 15 minutes, the middle heat level light flashes red. Once it's cool, empty the unburned pellets from the liner and start again. Never pour them back into the hopper: pellets that seem cool can still ignite others.

Turning it off

Press ON/OFF. The auger stops, but the fans keep running until the exhaust cools and the control board finishes the shutdown cycle. The manual says the panel lights go out, and that the Power light shows orange during shutdown.

heat.title: Setting the heat
heat.html:
Use the heat level Low and High buttons to set the heat. Five indicator lights show the setting, from #1 (bottom, low) to #5 (top, high).

Thermostat modes

The MAN-HI/LO-AUTO slide switch picks the mode. The stove comes from the factory in manual mode; the other two need an optional low voltage wall thermostat (not provided).

ManualBurns at your heat level until you change it or turn it off
HI/LOYour heat level while the thermostat calls for heat, then the lowest level
AUTOLike HI/LO, but shuts off after 45 minutes on the lowest level with no call for heat, and relights on the next call

On a thermostat, you still press ON/OFF for the first burn, and after the stove runs out of pellets and shuts off with a fault code. For power cuts, see Power outages.

Feed trim for different pellets

If low quality pellets let the fire go out during long periods on low, hold down the Auger button (the display changes to four lights on and one off) and press the up arrow for more feed. If low is still too warm on high energy pellets, press the down arrow instead. The factory setting is 3.

Trim changes the feed across the whole heat range. Be cautious and don't over-fire the stove. Never hand-feed pellets while it's running.

hopper.title: Pellets and the hopper
hopper.html:
Filling the hopper

Slide the stove top toward you to reach the hopper. Check for foreign objects before you fill it. To fill it completely, push the pellets to the back as you go. The hopper lid works a switch, so the auger won't run until the lid is completely closed.

Note: p. 9 says the hopper holds up to 65 pounds (29 Kg); p. 17 gives the hopper capacity as up to 60 pounds (28 Kg.) and adds that results vary with fuel density.
Maker's website: Hopper Capacity up to 60 lb.

What to burn

  • Premium wood pellets only. Pellets that meet or exceed PFI standards are recommended; ask your dealer for a pellet type.
  • In the U.S., burn only pellets graded by an EPA approved organization: Pellet Fuels Institute, ENplus or CANplus. In Canada, use premium grade pellets.
  • Avoid "dirty" fuel with dirt, chemical binders or high salt content. It hurts performance and voids the warranty.
  • Hardwood pellets generally make more ash than softwood. High-ash fuel can mean cleaning every day.
  • Never burn cordwood, garbage, rubber, plastics or flammable fluids.

Store pellets at least 48" (1.2 m) from the stove, in a cool, dry place.

clean.title: Burn pot, ash and glass
clean.html:
Shut the stove down, unplug it and let it go completely cold first. Open the door slowly (handle clockwise to horizontal) so ash isn't sucked out. A drop cloth helps catch spills.

Burn-pot liner: inspect daily

The holes in its bottom and sides feed air to the pellets, and impurities can form ash and hard clinkers that block them. Lift the liner out, scrape out clinkers, and clear the holes with a small pointed object if needed.

Burn pot

Check and vacuum it out after burning about 5 - 10 bags of pellets (the maintenance chart on p. 12 says every 5 bags). Put the liner back with its igniter hole toward the back, pushed against the igniter tube to seal it.

Ash

Brush ash into the bottom of the firebox and remove it with an ash or shop vacuum fitted with a fine dust filter. Never use a household vacuum, and never vacuum hot ash. Keep ashes in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid, on a non-combustible surface away from anything that burns.

Glass

When it's cool, wipe it with a soft cloth or paper towel and household glass cleaner or wood stove window cleaner. Don't use abrasive cleaners.

trouble.title: Flashing light or no fire
trouble.html:
If the stove shuts down unexpectedly, one of the heat level lights may be flashing:

#3 light flashingDidn't light, the fire went out, or the stove went cold while running
#4 light flashingHigh limit switch open: the stove overheated

Things you can check

  • No lights or fan noise after 30 sec.: make sure the power cord is plugged in, and check the household circuit breaker.
  • No pellets dropping: check that the hopper isn't empty and the lid is closed.
  • Pellets don't light after 8-10 min.: once the stove is shut down, unplugged and cold, make sure the burn pot and liner are installed properly, and clean the liner holes and igniter tube.
  • Goes out while running: low grade fuel may need more auger feed (see Set the heat), and the venting may need cleaning of ash build-up.

A tripped or faulty high limit switch, a damaged hopper lid switch, a faulty igniter, or a stove that won't turn off after the shutdown period are jobs for your dealer or service. Shutdown can take up to 20 min to cool, depending on how hot it was running.

power.title: Power outages and generators
power.html:
The stove plugs into a grounded three-prong, 120 volt, 60 Hz outlet. A surge protected power bar is recommended to protect its electronics from a power surge or lightning strike.

When the power comes back

  • Stove still hot: it goes into its start-up sequence and keeps running.
  • Stove cooled down: the exhaust blower runs for 10 minutes to purge any smoke. The first time the stove is plugged in, the combustion blower runs for 8-10 minutes; the manual calls this the same function.
  • On a thermostat in Auto mode: it won't start the ignition sequence until the thermostat calls for heat again.
Note: p. 10 says that in Auto mode the stove waits for the thermostat to call for heat before it restarts; p. 11 says that on a thermostat you must push ON/OFF when the electrical flow to the stove is interrupted.

Generators

The stove may run on a portable generator, but the generator's regulator may not suit the stove's electronics. The higher the quality of the generator (the smoother its output sine wave), the better the chance it works. Damage caused by power failures isn't covered by the warranty.

sounds.title: Normal sounds and first-fire smells
sounds.html:
Normal sounds

  • Rushing air and some small creaks when the blowers come on. The lower the burn rate, the slower the fans run.
  • Pellets dropping into the burn pot.
  • The auger motor pulsing on and off.
  • Now and then, a cracking noise as the auger cuts a pellet in half.

Fans

The two convection blowers come on once the stove warms up, change speed with the burn rate, and keep running after the stove shuts off until it has cooled down.

First fires

The high-temperature paint finishes curing during the first few times the stove burns on high, and some parts may be lightly coated with machining oil. Both can give off unpleasant odors. Open the windows to ventilate the room.

Some smoke inside the firebox during light-up is expected.

In extreme weather, if combustion changes dramatically, stop using the stove immediately.

service.title: Yearly cleaning and service
service.html:
The manual strongly recommends having the stove serviced annually by a trained professional.

Flue gas passagesAt least once a year, or every one to two tons of pellets (50-100 bags)
Exhaust ventingInspect at least twice every year; sweep the liner as needed
Venting cleaningAnnually or every two tons of pellets

High-ash pellets mean cleaning more often. During the heating season, check the venting for creosote: a layer of 3mm or more should be removed to reduce the risk of a chimney fire.

After a long shutdown, check the stove, its flue gas passages and the chimney liner for blockage before you relight.

Gaskets and glass

Check the rope gaskets around the door, window and ash pan now and then. Replace any that are loose, badly frayed or have a gap. If the glass cracks or breaks, it must be replaced before you use the stove, with 5 mm ceramic glass from your dealer; a qualified service technician should do it.

The blowers need cleaning too. The maintenance chart on p. 12 shows how often each part is checked, as a check-mark table.

safety.title: Safety and chimney fires
safety.html:
• Outside surfaces get hot enough to burn skin. Keep children, pets, clothing and furniture away, and supervise young children in the room.
  • Keep furniture, wood, paper, drapes and other combustibles, pellets included, 48" (122cm) from the front, 12" (30cm) from each side, and out of the fireplace enclosure.
  • Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or "freshen up" a fire.
  • Don't run the stove with the glass cracked, broken or removed. Put back any panel taken off for service first.
  • Don't over-fire it, and don't burn it with too little combustion air: creosote can form.
  • Smoke detectors are recommended. Follow your local code if it requires a smoke or CO detector in the same room.
Note: for the space in front of the stove, p. 5 says to keep furniture and other combustibles, pellet fuel included, 48" (122cm) from the front; the clearance list on p. 18 gives 36" [915mm] in front of the unit.

Chimney or vent fire

  1. Call the local fire department.
  2. Put out the fire in the burn-pot liner with a cup of water and close the door.
  3. Check the flue liner, chimney, attic and roof for anything hot enough to catch fire. Use a fire extinguisher or garden hose if needed.
  4. Don't use the stove again until you're certain the chimney and its lining aren't damaged.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
True North warrants the stove to the original consumer:

Firebox, castings, glass3 years parts (1 year labour)
Electrical components and switches1 year parts and labour
Gaskets, paint (peeling), bricks, firebox liner, burn pot and liner1 year (parts only)

Glass is covered for thermal breakage only, not impact. The warranty isn't transferable, covers brand new products only, and applies to normal residential use. To make a claim, give your True North dealer the dated bill of sale, the model name and the serial number.

Not covered

  • Misuse, abuse, improper installation, lack of maintenance, over firing, negligence, power failures, downdrafts or venting problems
  • Burning materials the stove isn't EPA certified for, or not running it according to the owner's manual
  • Scratches, corrosion, warping or discoloration from over firing, abrasives or chemical cleaners
  • Unauthorized parts, or installation not done by an authorized qualified technician
A one-time replacement limit applies to all warranted parts. The warranty text in the manual is dated June 1, 2016.

specOutput.title: Heat output and input
specOutput.html:
EPA tested BTU output6,000 to 25,600 BTU/hr.
Input (p. 4)approx. 10,000 to 38,000 Btu (depending on fuel type)
Input (rating label)11,000 - 39,000 Btu/Hr
Pellet heat valuejust under 7,000 to almost 9,000 Btu/lb.
Maker's website: BTU High 36,000; BTU Low 8,000.

The output range is based on CSA B415 efficiency testing and the EPA test burn rates. The manufacturer-set minimum low burn must not be altered; doing so is against federal regulations.

Note: p. 4 gives the input rating as approx. 10,000 to 38,000 Btu (depending on fuel type); the rating label on p. 31 gives 11,000 - 39,000 Btu/Hr.

specEpa.title: Emissions and efficiency
specEpa.html:
EPA certified emissions0.69g/hr
HHV tested efficiency73%
LHV tested efficiency79.6%

Meets the 2020 U.S. EPA PM limits using premium wood pellets. Efficiencies are weighted averages tested to CSA B415. The rating label (p. 31) reads: tested to method 28R and ASTM E2779-10 using PFI graded premium wood pellets, 0.7 g/hr.

Safety testing by Intertek Testing Services NA Ltd. (ETL#4001507): listed room heater, pellet fuel-burning type, and the label adds "also for use in Mobile Homes".

specElec.html:

Peak4.3 Amps
Normal operating2.5 Amps

Three-prong grounding plug: plug directly into a properly grounded three-prong, 120 volt, 60 Hz receptacle and never cut or remove the grounding prong. Don't route the cord under or in front of the appliance or against hot or sharp surfaces. A surge protected power bar is recommended. The wiring diagram on p. 27 shows the main board and its fuses as a drawing.

specVent.title: Venting
specVent.html:
LinerUL 1777/ULC S635 or ULC S640 conforming 3"(76mm) or 4"(102mm) stainless steel
Flue collar3" (increaser needed for 4" liner)
Maximum vent length45ft (13.5m)
Over 4000 feet4"(102mm) pellet vent suggested
Outside air2"(51mm) ID non-combustible pipe

The combustion blower pressurizes the vent: silicone the vent pipe and fasten it to the starter pipe with three screws; if the liner has no locking system, screw every joint with three screws, and seal joints with high temperature silicone or aluminium tape if required. No flue damper, no flue serving another appliance, no air distribution duct work.

Canada requires a full flue liner to the chimney top; the USA also allows a direct flue connection. A factory-built fireplace needs a full stainless rigid or flexible liner (UL1777 U.S. / ULC S635 Canada). A clean-out tee sits at the horizontal-to-vertical transition.

Note: p. 19 and the rating label (p. 31) give the liner standard as UL 1777/ULC S635 or ULC S640; for the full liner required in Canada, p. 20 gives CAN/ULC-B365 or CAN/ULC-S640.

Input: 'Aprox. 10,000Btu to 38,000 (Depending on fuel type)' on p. 4 vs 'INPUT 11,000 - 39,000 Btu/Hr' on the rating label, p. 31.
Current: 4.3 Amps peak / 2.5 Amps normal operating on p. 4 vs 120V A/C, 4.1AMP on the rating label, p. 31.
Rating label location: 'On top of the Hopper Cover' (p. 4) vs 'located on the back of the hopper' (p. 31).
Front: clearance list gives 'In Front of unit 36" [915mm]' (p. 18); warnings say never place combustibles incl. pellet fuel within 48" (122cm) of the front (p. 5).

Front clearance in the owner safety drawer (the same difference as the specClear entry; the clearance card carries a short note too): warnings say never place combustibles incl. pellet fuel within 48" (122cm) of the front (p. 5); the clearance list gives 'In Front of unit 36" [915mm]' (p. 18).

Other-sides hearth: the rating label (p. 31) gives the minimum hearth on the other sides, measured from the fireplace opening, as 200 MM / 6 in; the mm and inch figures don't match and no other page gives this figure. Ember protection (if required, measured from the firebox viewing door) is a different measurement: 6" (150mm) in the p. 18 text and 6"/152mm in Figure 12 on p. 20.

Thermostat restart after a power loss: p. 10 says in Auto mode the stove won't start ignition until the thermostat calls for heat again; p. 11 says on a thermostat ON/OFF must be pushed when the electrical flow to the stove is interrupted.

review.notes: Maintenance chart (p. 12) is a weekly/monthly/yearly check-mark grid whose column positions are lost in the text; only its written notes (e.g. burn pot 'or Every 5 bags', liner 'Daily') were used. Stove dimensions (Fig. 9, p. 17), the clearance drawing (Fig. 11, p. 18) and the wiring diagram (Fig. 20, p. 27; values 2 A., 2 A., 3 A., 5 A. not mapped to circuits) are drawings and were not transcribed. Fig. 11's metric labels (380mm, 203mm) differ from the p. 18 list (330mm, 216mm), which matches the rating label; inch values agree; list values used. Minor differences shown inline rather than flagged: emissions 0.69g/hr (p. 4) vs 0.7 g/hr (label p. 31); first plug-in blower run 8-10 minutes (p. 9) vs 10 minute purge after a cold outage (p. 10); burn pot every 5 bags (chart p. 12) vs about 5 - 10 bags (p. 13); at shutdown 'control panel lights will go out' (p. 9) vs Power light 'orange during shutdown' (p. 8). Manual cross-references are off: thermostat operation cited as page 19 (it is p. 11), wiring diagram as page 25 (p. 27), and figure numbers off by one on pp. 14, 15, 22 and 24. p. 4 prints 'ULC 628S' (cover: ULC S628; label: ULC S628-93). Damper readings printed '0.10-0.12n.w.c.' and '0.09" to 0.11"'. Label says 'also for use in Mobile Homes' but the manual has no mobile-home installation section, so none is given. Catalog features 'self-cleaning' burn pot liner and 'air-wash glass' are not described in the manual; glass_area_sq_in (104) is not stated (the manual gives only replacement glass 9-1/4"(235mm) x 13-1/4"(337mm) x 5 mm). Troubleshooting chart row pairing for 'Combustion Blower blocked or damaged' is ambiguous in the text, so it is grouped with the vacuum-switch row's checks. The manual (written by Pacific Energy, True North's maker) says installation and repair are for a qualified technician (p. 12) yet describes owner cleaning; owner drawers keep its shut-down, unplugged and cold rule. No French-only or scrambled text affected the content.
